claims.text: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between a thermodynamic driving force for Cr–Al chemical ordering and kinetic limitations on atomic diffusion.
Chemical ordering partitions the high-temperature BCC phase into ordered B2 regions embedded in a disordered BCC matrix.
The ordered B2 regions are nanoscale.
The ordered B2 regions are enriched in Cr and Al.
Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially be processed as a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase.
Annealing temperature and duration should be varied systematically, with a reduced-Cr or Co-for-Cr composition used as a control.
The approximately 900–1100 °C window provides sufficient atomic mobility for ordering without producing complete equilibrium phase separation.
Composition and annealing temperature determine the length scale of B2 plus BCC decomposition in Al–Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys.
Cr substitution for Co promotes decomposition into ordered B2 and disordered BCC phases.
A strong negative mixing enthalpy between Cr and Al promotes local chemical ordering.
Cr–Al chemical interactions promote nucleation of ordered B2 within the BCC matrix.
Incomplete atomic diffusion limits the spatial scale of the B2/BCC transformation.
Kinetic hindrance stabilizes a metastable B2-plus-BCC microstructure under selected thermal conditions.
Prolonged annealing of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 at 900–1100 °C should produce detectable B2 regions in a BCC matrix.
A lower-Cr control should show significantly reduced or delayed formation of the ordered phase.
The pre-annealing baseline is a homogeneous BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy and an analogous homogeneous BCC control alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies only where diffusion permits local ordering but not complete equilibrium phase separation.
Very rapid cooling or extremely prolonged annealing can move the alloy outside the proposed kinetic regime.
Failure to detect B2 ordering or a Cr-dependent difference under the specified treatments would falsify the proposed Cr–Al-ordering mechanism.
